evidence.title: Win25H2Clean Session Manager Power baseline export
evidence.summary: A clean VM baseline export confirmed WatchdogResumeTimeout = 120 and WatchdogSleepTimeout = 300 under Session Manager\Power, with adjacent PowerSettingProfile = 0.

evidence.title: Current-build ntoskrnl Ghidra fallback for the watchdog timeout pair
evidence.summary: The current-build ntoskrnl.exe pass found exact string hits for WatchdogResumeTimeout and WatchdogSleepTimeout and preserved reviewable fallback artifacts for the next-gate watchdog lane.

evidence.title: Repo PoFxInitPowerManagement pseudocode lead
evidence.summary: The repo-side pseudocode ties PopWatchdogResumeTimeout and PopWatchdogSleepTimeout to the directed power-up and directed power-down watchdog timeout globals, giving the pair a subsystem-level semantic lead.

evidence.title: Win25H2Clean reboot-verified watchdog timeout boot trace
evidence.summary: A successful host-driven boot trace on the current visible-shell baseline confirmed a real reboot cycle, preserved the same 120/300 values after boot, and kept shell health intact.

evidence.title: Host-side ETL registry review for Session Manager Power
evidence.summary: A filtered xperf dump of the successful boot trace proved repeated boot-time access to Session Manager\Power by System and later svchost.exe, with adjacent SystemPowerPolicy and ShutdownOccurred activity. The exact watchdog pair names were still absent in the parsed event payloads.

evidence.title: Win25H2Clean Procmon boot-log review for Session Manager Power
evidence.summary: A baseline-only Procmon boot-log lane successfully converted a large boot PML and CSV, then filtered 18 hits from System on adjacent Session Manager\Power values such as SystemPowerPolicy and ShutdownOccurred. The exact watchdog pair still did not appear in the filtered Procmon boot-log hits.

evidence.title: Win25H2Clean sleep capability for the watchdog lane
evidence.summary: The current VMware baseline exposes only Standby (S1). S3, hibernate, and S0 low power idle are unavailable, which constrains the next exact live-read attempt to an S1 transition or a different environment.

evidence.title: DcomLaunch attribution for the watchdog svchost lead
evidence.summary: The ETL svchost lead was narrowed to the DcomLaunch service host group, and the current VM baseline confirmed that the same group hosts the Power service.

evidence.title: Targeted post-boot Procmon trigger for the DcomLaunch Power lane
evidence.summary: A shell-safe post-boot Procmon capture targeted the DcomLaunch/Power lane with tasklist, powercfg, and service queries. It produced a real PML and CSV but still returned zero matching reads for the watchdog pair or adjacent Session Manager Power values.

evidence.title: S1-specific Procmon follow-up for the watchdog lane
evidence.summary: An S1-specific Procmon attempt tried to force the only available sleep state on the current VMware baseline. Shell health recovered, but the guest-ops channel dropped during the transition, no usable in-guest Procmon artifacts survived, wake history stayed at zero, and post-checks did not show a fresh sleep/resume Kernel-Power event.

evidence.title: S1 scheduled-task Procmon follow-up for the watchdog lane
evidence.summary: A second S1-specific attempt moved the payload into a guest-side scheduled task so the host no longer depended on a long-lived guest-ops session. The lane still produced no usable in-guest artifacts, the task was not present when queried after recovery, wake history stayed at zero, and no fresh sleep/resume Kernel-Power output appeared.

evidence.title: Tools-hardened lightweight ETW S1 follow-up for the watchdog lane
evidence.summary: A tools-hardened lightweight ETW follow-up retried the watchdog lane with split trace phases on RegProbe-Baseline-ToolsHardened-20260330. The VM still exposed only S1, and the guest dropped out during the sleep transition before a usable exact-value ETW bundle could be completed.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD value follow-up for the watchdog timeout pair
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD follow-up resolved the live watchdog globals on the running guest, read `PopWatchdogResumeTimeout = 120` and `PopWatchdogSleepTimeout = 300`, and also read the derived directed-power globals `PopFxDirectedPowerUpTimeoutMs = 240000` and `PopFxDirectedPowerDownTimeoutMs = 420000`, matching the repo PoFx pseudocode relation `(timeout + 120) * 1000`.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD disassembly for the watchdog timeout path
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD disassembly follow-up showed `PopComputeWatchdogTimeout` selecting directly between `PopWatchdogSleepTimeout` and `PopWatchdogResumeTimeout` on the running guest, and showed `PopUpdatePowerActionWatchdogTimeouts` refreshing the adjacent power-action watchdog globals from either diagnostic override constants or the default watchdog globals.

evidence.title: Linux KVM Procmon power-burst replay for the watchdog timeout pair
evidence.summary: A reusable Linux KVM `watchdog-power-burst` Procmon replay exported a 260953-row CSV, preserved the original `WatchdogSleepTimeout = 300` value before and after the burst, and still returned zero hits for the watchdog pair and broader Session Manager\Power fragments.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD registry-helper follow-up for the watchdog timeout pair
evidence.location: evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/local-kd-watchdog-reg-helpers-20260407abc/watchdog-symbol-sweep-20260407a-summary.json and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/local-kd-watchdog-reg-helpers-20260407abc/watchdog-symbol-sweep-20260407a.log and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/local-kd-watchdog-reg-helpers-20260407abc/watchdog-reader-disasm-20260407b-summary.json and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/local-kd-watchdog-reg-helpers-20260407abc/watchdog-reader-disasm-20260407b.log and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/local-kd-watchdog-reg-helpers-20260407abc/watchdog-xref-remap-20260407c-summary.json and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/local-kd-watchdog-reg-helpers-20260407abc/watchdog-xref-remap-20260407c.log and research/notes/power-session-watchdog-timeouts-kvm-local-kd-reg-helper-follow-up-20260407.md
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD helper-family pass resolved `PopReadRegKeyValue`, `PopOpenPowerKey`, and `PopReadUlongPowerKey`, showed that `PopReadRegKeyValue` issues `ZwOpenKey` and `ZwQueryValueKey` on behalf of power-manager callers, showed that `PopOpenPowerKey` roots itself on `PopRegKey`, and remapped the older fallback watchdog xref offsets into unrelated PnP driver-init code rather than a watchdog reader.

evidence.title: Incident review for S1 watchdog timeout runtime attempts
evidence.summary: Incident reviewed: the retained direct S1 Procmon, scheduled-task S1 Procmon, and tools-hardened lightweight ETW S1 failures are classified as validation-environment limitations. Shell recovered where post-checks were possible, rollback was not required, and the incidents do not provide safety proof or decisive exact-value runtime-read proof for the watchdog pair.

evidence.title: Kernel power next-gate intake summary
evidence.summary: The 2026-03-28 intake review ranked the watchdog pair above the Executive worker-thread values because the baseline existence, exact string hits, and Ghidra artifacts were already stronger.

evidence.title: KVM ETW stackwalk captures exact WatchdogResumeTimeout RegQueryValue
evidence.summary: After fixing the host ETW stackwalk ingest path to backfill guest-generated tracerpt XML when host-side tracerpt is unavailable, a QGA-launched 45-second capture produced a physical ETL, XML sidecar, and normalized bundle for `WatchdogResumeTimeout`. The bundle contains one exact `RegQueryValue` event for `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Power` / `WatchdogResumeTimeout`, with caller stack frames through `reg.exe`, `KernelBase.dll`, `ntdll.dll`, and `ntoskrnl.exe`; the helper registry probe returned `REG_DWORD 0x78`, matching the retained baseline and KD value of 120. This upgrades the pair from no exact live read to partial exact-read proof.

validation_proof.exact_quote_or_path: The tools-hardened lightweight ETW follow-up confirmed that S1 is available on this VM, but the sleep transition still pushed VMware Tools and the guest shell out before a usable exact-value ETW bundle could be completed, so the current environment still cannot close the watchdog lane decisively.
validation_proof.notes: The runtime story now includes the ETL review, the Procmon boot-log review, a targeted post-boot DcomLaunch/Power trigger, two older S1-specific Procmon attempts, a newer tools-hardened lightweight ETW follow-up, and a 2026-04-23 exact helper-triggered ETW query for `WatchdogResumeTimeout`. The pair is now decisively real on the current build, but the sleep-side exact read and the watchdog-specific caller into `PopReadRegKeyValue` remain open.

records.name: Disable Application Compatibility Engine and SwitchBack
records.summary: Two AppCompat.admx policy values written by the app under HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AppCompat: SbEnable (SwitchBack) and DisableEngine (Application Compatibility Engine). Both come from the same policy family and the same registry root. VM Procmon capture on 2026-03-26 in Win25H2Clean confirmed powershell.exe writes DisableEngine=REG_DWORD 0x1 and SbEnable=REG_DWORD 0x0, then reg.exe reads both values back successfully. Microsoft Learn CSP page (Policy CSP - ADMX_AppCompat) confirms both policies exist on Windows 11 21H2+. SbEnable is now also published as a standalone record in privacy.disable-switchback.policy; this record keeps it for bundle-audit context because the current app still writes both values together.

decision.why: Both values are proven in three layers: local ADMX semantics, the Microsoft Learn ADMX_AppCompat CSP page, and VM Procmon capture showing direct writes and read-backs for DisableEngine=1 and SbEnable=0 under HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AppCompat in Win25H2Clean. This is app-ready evidence-wise, but it stays non-default because Microsoft ADML warns that disabling the Application Compatibility Engine can cause BSOD with old antivirus or other security software.

app_current_implementation.notes: The app writes both values as part of the broader application-compatibility policy path. Paths and values match local AppCompat.admx. SbEnable is now documented separately in privacy.disable-switchback.policy for standalone publication, but it remains here because the current app still writes it together with DisableEngine. The app also writes four AppDeviceInventory values and DisablePCA in the same code path; those are tracked in separate records.

targets.notes: Windows default is missing (key absent). SbEnable is the cleanest proven value in this record. VM Procmon capture on 2026-03-26 in Win25H2Clean confirmed powershell.exe writes SbEnable=REG_DWORD 0x0 and reg.exe reads it back. Numeric direction is fully proven. Standalone publication guidance now lives in privacy.disable-switchback.policy; this target remains here to document the current combined app bundle.

records.name: Disable App Device Inventory Policies
records.summary: Four AppDeviceInventory policy values written by the app under HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AppCompat. All four come from the same policy family (AppDeviceInventory.admx), share the same registry root, and have explicit enabledValue=1 / disabledValue=0 blocks in the local ADMX. Microsoft Learn CSP page (Policy CSP - AppDeviceInventory) confirms these policies exist. VM Procmon capture on 2026-03-26 in Win25H2Clean confirmed powershell.exe writes all four values under HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AppCompat and reg.exe reads them back successfully. Derived from the former mixed application-compatibility policy record on 2026-03-13.

decision.why: All four values are now confirmed in three layers: local AppDeviceInventory.admx (explicit enabledValue=1), the Microsoft Learn CSP page, and VM Procmon capture showing direct writes and read-backs for all four values under HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AppCompat in Win25H2Clean. Risk is low because these policies reduce telemetry collection rather than core application compatibility behavior. Pre-24H2 systems may ignore the keys, but that is a scope caveat rather than a safety blocker.

app_current_implementation.notes: The app writes all four values as part of the broader application-compatibility policy path. Path and values match both local AppDeviceInventory.admx and the CSP page. The app still writes DisableEngine, SbEnable, and DisablePCA in the same code path; those are tracked in separate records.

records.summary: Officially documented user environment-variable bundle for opting PowerShell and the .NET CLI out of telemetry. Good for privacy-focused shell workflows, but it can reduce telemetry available for product improvement and support diagnostics.

decision.why: Microsoft directly documents POWERSHELL_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT and DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT as supported opt-out environment variables, and documents that persistent user environment variables are stored under HKEY_USERS\<user>\Environment, which corresponds to HKCU\Environment for the current user. The app writes the documented opt-out value 1 for both variables on that exact user environment surface.

targets.notes: HKCU/Environment is the current-user view of the persistent user environment-variable store.

records.name: Disable PCA Compatibility Diagnostics Detection
records.summary: Controls whether Windows Program Compatibility Assistant (PCA) detects compatibility issues for applications and drivers. Value name: DisablePcaUI under HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AppCompat. Policy family: pca.admx (DisablePcaUIPolicy). Supported on Windows 8+. enabledValue=1 means detection stays active and disabledValue=0 turns detection off.

decision.why: The proof chain is complete: pca.admx provides explicit enabledValue and disabledValue mappings, pca.adml provides exact behavior text, and the Microsoft Learn CSP page confirms the policy surface. Numeric direction is explicit and does not rely on inference. Risk is low because this disables diagnostics detection rather than disabling PCA entirely. recommended_for_general_users remains false because the practical benefit is small and the setting needs context to use responsibly.

app_current_implementation.notes: The current app research-surface manifest defaults this card to DisablePcaUI = 0 on the documented policy path, preserving the validated disabledValue state while keeping the record_id bound to the surfaced card.

targets.notes: WARNING: value name 'DisablePcaUI' is semantically inverted relative to its behavior. To disable detection, write 0 (disabledValue), not 1. Writing 1 (enabledValue) keeps detection active. This is consistent with pca.admx but counterintuitive from the value name alone. Do not confuse with DisablePCA (separate key, same path) which actually disables PCA entirely.

records.name: Disable SwitchBack Compatibility Policy
records.summary: Controls the SwitchBack policy under HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AppCompat. SwitchBack allows applications that detect Windows Vista or later to also receive compatibility fixes normally reserved for older OS versions. SbEnable=0 disables this behavior. Extracted from privacy.disable-appcompat-engine.policy on 2026-03-13 because SbEnable is individually proven and does not carry the Microsoft-documented BSOD risk tied to DisableEngine in the parent bundle. AppCompat.admx has explicit enabledValue=0 and disabledValue=1 for SbEnable, the Microsoft Learn CSP page confirms the policy exists, and VM Procmon capture on 2026-03-26 in Win25H2Clean confirmed powershell.exe writes SbEnable=REG_DWORD 0x0 and reg.exe reads it back.

decision.why: Proof chain is complete and no comparable BSOD or engine-wide compatibility risk is documented for SbEnable. AppCompat.admx provides explicit enabledValue=0, the Microsoft Learn CSP page confirms policy existence and scope, and Procmon confirmed the runtime write. recommended_for_general_users remains false because the practical benefit is small and most users do not need to manage this policy explicitly.

app_current_implementation.notes: The current app research-surface manifest defaults this card to SbEnable = 0, preserving the documented SwitchBack-off state while keeping the record_id bound to the surfaced card.

targets.notes: Windows default is missing (key absent). Missing behaves identically to value=1. Explicit enabledValue=0 in AppCompat.admx proves numeric direction without context inference. No BSOD risk is documented for SbEnable alone; that warning belongs to DisableEngine in the parent bundle.

records.name: Set Diagnostic Data to Minimum Supported Level
records.summary: The app writes AllowTelemetry = 0 on the documented policy path and now gates the tweak to Enterprise, Education, IoT Enterprise, and Server-class editions. Microsoft documents that value 0 is only supported on those edition families, so the app no longer offers it as a general-purpose one-click switch on unsupported SKUs.

decision.why: The official mapping is clear, the app writes the documented policy path, and unsupported editions now return NotApplicable instead of applying value 0 blindly. This makes the tweak app-ready while still keeping it non-default because the supported meaning is edition-limited.

app_current_implementation.notes: The research app-surface card keeps the current app's edition-aware gate. It writes AllowTelemetry = 0 only when the local edition matches the documented supported families and returns NotApplicable on unsupported SKUs.

records.name: Exploit Protection System Mitigations
records.summary: Microsoft documents exploit protection system mitigations through the Windows Security app, the ProcessMitigation PowerShell cmdlets, and an Exploit Guard policy that points to an XML configuration file. The app now imports the documented XML policy surface instead of writing raw MitigationOptions and MitigationAuditOptions blobs directly under the kernel registry path.

decision.why: Microsoft's documented exploit protection surface is XML, Windows Security, and the ProcessMitigation cmdlets. The app imports the documented XML baseline and restores from a captured backup XML through the same command surface, so this is app-ready evidence-wise. It still stays non-default because exploit protection changes can affect application compatibility.

app_current_implementation.notes: The app now stages the checked-in Exploit Protection XML baseline to %TEMP%\RegProbe\ExploitProtection\security-disable-system-mitigations.xml and imports it via Set-ProcessMitigation -PolicyFilePath. Rollback restores the exported backup XML via the same documented import path. The raw MitigationOptions and MitigationAuditOptions kernel blobs were removed from the provider.

writes.notes: The app stages the checked-in XML resource to a temp file and imports it through the documented ProcessMitigation surface.

decision.why: The local Microsoft GameDVR.admx file explicitly defines AllowGameDVR under Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\GameDVR with valueName AllowGameDVR, and the paired ADML help text states that disabling the setting prevents Windows Game Recording while enabled or not configured allows recording and broadcasting. The app writes that documented disabled state.

records.name: Wallpaper JPEG Import Quality
records.summary: The current build evidence for JPEGImportQuality now lines up across decomp, Procmon, and repeated Win25H2Clean runtime probes: shell32.dll carries the JPEGImportQuality transcode path, Explorer.EXE queried JPEGImportQuality = 100 during a shell-driven wallpaper apply, the v3.1 runtime lane re-applied a JPEG wallpaper with a fresh WPR capture and restored the original wallpaper, the missing baseline restores cleanly, and the current app writes the same 100 state.

decision.why: shell32.dll decompiled to the JPEGImportQuality transcode path, Explorer.EXE queried JPEGImportQuality = 100 in a shell-driven Procmon pass on Win25H2Clean, the v3.1 runtime lane re-applied a JPEG wallpaper with a fresh WPR capture and clean shell health, the reversible VM probe confirmed missing -> 100 -> missing, and the current app writes the same value with a clean restore story. That is enough to treat the current value 100 profile as app-ready even though the setting is not published by Microsoft as a registry contract.

records.area: Feature Setting vs Observed Registry Setting
records.summary: Microsoft documents the Restart apps sign-in feature, and a guest-side reversible probe on Win25H2Clean confirmed the raw RestartApps registry mapping under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon. decision.why: The guest-side reversible probe on Win25H2Clean confirmed the raw RestartApps registry mapping: missing, 1, and 0 are all observable states, and 0 disables automatic app restart after sign-in. The current app write now matches the observed off state.

app_current_implementation.notes: The current app writes RestartApps = 0, and the guest probe confirmed that 0 disables automatic app restart after sign-in on Win25H2Clean.

records.name: Executive Additional Worker Threads
records.summary: Validated cross-layer record. The Session Manager Executive worker-thread pair now has a clean baseline export on Win25H2Clean, a bounded boot-time ETL extract that proves runtime access to Session Manager\Executive, exact current-build ntoskrnl string hits, preserved Ghidra fallback artifacts, a supporting ReactOS semantic hypothesis, a tools-hardened lightweight ETW follow-up that produced exact RegQueryValue hits for both AdditionalCriticalWorkerThreads and AdditionalDelayedWorkerThreads under a concurrent I/O and process-burst trigger, a later host-driven KVM Procmon replay that stayed at zero exact-target hits on the working guest, a later hardened-runner KVM Procmon replay that again stayed at zero exact-target hits under the same Executive burst, a KVM local-KD wildcard that resolved the live `ExpAdditionalCriticalWorkerThreads` / `ExpAdditionalDelayedWorkerThreads` data symbols, and a KVM local-KD value dump that showed the same live pair still at `0 / 0`. That is enough for Class A within this project even though the lane remains research-only and non-actionable in the app.

decision.why: The Executive worker-thread pair now has a clean baseline export, a bounded boot-time ETL extract that proves early Session Manager\Executive activity from System (PID 4), exact current-build ntoskrnl string hits, current-build Ghidra fallback artifacts, a supporting live KVM local-KD symbol query for the exact `ExpAdditional*` data names, a matching live KVM value dump that still shows the pair at `0 / 0`, and a tools-hardened lightweight ETW follow-up that produced exact RegQueryValue hits for both AdditionalCriticalWorkerThreads and AdditionalDelayedWorkerThreads under a concurrent burst trigger. That is enough for Class A within this project even though the lane remains research-only and not app-actionable.

app_current_implementation.notes: The app now surfaces the validated Session Manager Executive worker-thread pair as a research-card batch.

targets.notes: Keep the pair together. The lane is stronger when AdditionalCriticalWorkerThreads and AdditionalDelayedWorkerThreads are treated as one candidate surface.

records.name: Executive UUID Sequence Number
records.summary: Validated cross-layer record for UuidSequenceNumber under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Executive. The clean Win25H2Clean baseline confirmed the live value, the residual static triage found an exact current-build ntoskrnl.exe Unicode hit, later KVM full-analysis replays confirmed that the string still exists but did not recover a direct or bounded indirect ntoskrnl code reference, the bounded Executive ETL review proved adjacent query and set activity for the same value during early boot, and later KVM local-KD follow-ups resolved both the live UUID symbol family and the current-build load/save path that opens a Session Manager Executive persisted-state location and queries or sets the `UuidSequenceNumber` value name. A deeper KVM local-KD value dump also showed live current-build in-memory UUID state on the working guest, and a later trigger-state follow-up wrapped the existing UUID / RPC / COM burst between two local-KD snapshots but still observed no delta: `ExpUuidSequenceNumber = 0x002caf1b`, `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid = 1`, and `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved = 0` before and after the trigger. A subsequent API-level local-KD disassembly then showed that `ExUuidCreate` funnels into `ExpUuidGetValues`, `NtAllocateUuids` funnels into `ExpAllocateUuids`, and `ExpAllocateUuids` can update `ExpUuidSequenceNumber` and set `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved = 1` before `ExpUuidSaveSequenceNumberIf` runs. A direct user-mode API trigger built around repeated `UuidCreateSequential` plus `NtAllocateUuids` calls then also completed cleanly and still produced no state delta in the same local-KD snapshot lane. A follow-up seed and Config Manager disassembly then showed `NtSetUuidSeed` as a privileged seed-write path with `SeAccessCheck` and cache updates, while `CmpUuidCreate` turned out to be only a retry wrapper around `ExUuidCreate`. A later forced-invalid local-KD follow-up then cleared `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid` to `0`, reran the same direct API burst, and observed `ExpUuidSequenceNumber` advance from `0x002caf1b` to `0x002caf1c` while `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid` returned to `1` and `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved` stayed `0`. A later same-run forced-invalid follow-up then observed both the live kernel state and the stored `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Executive\UuidSequenceNumber` value advance from `0x002caf1d` to `0x002caf1e` in the same trigger window. A later hardened-runner KVM Procmon replay then ensured an elevated guest shell, exported `240500` rows under the alternate Executive burst, and still returned zero `Session Manager\Executive` or `UuidSequenceNumber` hits. A later bounded exact-read Procmon diagnostic then showed that both a minimal custom control replay and the stronger direct UUID API replay fail at `Procmon SaveAs` on the working KVM guest. Runtime ETW and KVM Procmon lanes therefore stayed at zero exact-target hits even after the same-run kernel-plus-registry state-transition proof under local-KD. A later QGA-launched WPR boot-registry rerun then completed a real reboot cycle, retained exact quoted `UuidSequenceNumber` `QueryValue` and `SetValue` lines, and closed the remaining direct runtime-read gap. That is enough for Class A in this project even though the value remains research-only and not app-mapped.

decision.why: UuidSequenceNumber now has converged project evidence: clean baseline existence, an exact current-build ntoskrnl string hit, bounded early-boot ETL evidence in the same Session Manager Executive path, a live KVM local-KD wildcard plus disassembly that resolve the current-build UUID load/save/state family and tie it to the exact `UuidSequenceNumber` value name, a same-run forced-invalid follow-up that shows both the live kernel state and stored registry value advance together by `+1`, and now a QGA-launched WPR boot-registry trace that retains exact quoted `QueryValue` plus `SetValue` lines for `UuidSequenceNumber` during boot. The WPR normalizer binds those retained exact-value hits to the intended Session Manager Executive target path supplied to the run, and that path was already independently corroborated by the earlier bounded ETL review and local-KD disassembly. That is enough for Class A in this project even though the value remains research-only and not app-mapped.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD wildcard for the UuidSequenceNumber symbol family
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD wildcard follow-up attached to the live guest kernel and resolved the current-build `ExpUuidLoadSequenceNumber`, `ExpUuidSaveSequenceNumber`, `ExpUuidSequenceNumber`, `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid`, `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved`, and `ExpUuidSequenceNumberRegName` symbol family in the running guest.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD disassembly for the UuidSequenceNumber path
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD follow-up disassembled `ExpUuidLoadSequenceNumber` and `ExpUuidSaveSequenceNumber`, showing a live current-build path through `RtlGetPersistedStateLocation`, `ZwOpenKey`, `ZwQueryValueKey` / `ZwSetValueKey`, and the `ExpUuidSequenceNumberRegName` buffer. The same run resolved the path-builder strings to `\Registry\Machine\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Executive` plus `KernelExecutive`, and resolved the live value-name buffer to `UuidSequenceNumber`.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD value dump for UuidSequenceNumber state
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD value dump read `ExpUuidSequenceNumber = 0x002caf0c`, `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid = 1`, and `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved = 0` from the running guest kernel, showing live UUID state that stays within +3 of the earlier guest-side registry sample.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD trigger-state follow-up for UuidSequenceNumber
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD follow-up wrapped the existing `uuid-rpc-com-burst` trigger between two live kernel snapshots and still observed no delta: `ExpUuidSequenceNumber = 0x002caf1b`, `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid = 1`, and `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved = 0` before and after the burst.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD API disassembly for UuidSequenceNumber allocation paths
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD API follow-up showed `ExUuidCreate` calling `ExpUuidGetValues`, `NtAllocateUuids` calling `ExpAllocateUuids`, and `ExpAllocateUuids` itself updating `ExpUuidSequenceNumber`, `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid`, and `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved`, which makes direct UUID allocation APIs better future trigger candidates than the generic UUID / RPC / COM burst.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD direct API trigger follow-up for UuidSequenceNumber
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD follow-up ran repeated `UuidCreateSequential` and `NtAllocateUuids` calls from guest PowerShell with clean trigger exit code 0, but still observed no state delta: `ExpUuidSequenceNumber = 0x002caf1b`, `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid = 1`, and `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved = 0` before and after the direct API burst.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD seed and Config Manager follow-up for UuidSequenceNumber
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD follow-up showed `NtSetUuidSeed` as a privileged seed-write path with `SeAccessCheck`, cache writes, and `ExpUuidCacheValid` updates, while `CmpUuidCreate` resolved as a retry wrapper around `ExUuidCreate` rather than a separate persisted-state reader for `UuidSequenceNumber`.

evidence.title: Linux KVM local-KD forced-invalid trigger follow-up for UuidSequenceNumber
evidence.summary: A debugger-assisted KVM local-KD follow-up forced `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid` to `0`, reran the direct `UuidCreateSequential` plus `NtAllocateUuids` burst, and observed `ExpUuidSequenceNumber` advance from `0x002caf1b` to `0x002caf1c` while `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid` returned to `1` and `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved` stayed `0`.

evidence.title: Linux KVM guest-side regstate follow-up for the forced-invalid UUID trigger
evidence.summary: A same-run forced-invalid follow-up paired guest-side registry sampling with local-KD state capture and observed both `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Executive\UuidSequenceNumber` and `nt!ExpUuidSequenceNumber` advance from `0x2caf1d` to `0x2caf1e` while `ExpUuidSequenceNumberValid` returned to `1` and `ExpUuidSequenceNumberNotSaved` stayed `0`.

evidence.title: Linux KVM bounded Procmon SaveAs timeout follow-up for UuidSequenceNumber
evidence.location: evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/procmon-saveas-timeout-kvm-20260407u6/u6-summary.json and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/procmon-saveas-timeout-kvm-20260407u6/u6-probe-stage.json and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/procmon-saveas-timeout-kvm-20260407u6/u6.txt and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/procmon-saveas-timeout-kvm-20260407u6/host-review.json and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/uuidsequence-procmon-saveas-timeout-kvm-20260407u7/u7-summary.json and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/uuidsequence-procmon-saveas-timeout-kvm-20260407u7/u7-probe-stage.json and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/uuidsequence-procmon-saveas-timeout-kvm-20260407u7/u7.txt and evidence/files/vm-tooling-staging/uuidsequence-procmon-saveas-timeout-kvm-20260407u7/host-review.json and research/notes/system-executive-uuid-sequence-number-kvm-procmon-saveas-timeout-follow-up-20260407.md
evidence.summary: A bounded KVM Procmon diagnostic retried the intended Session Manager Executive exact-read lane twice: once with a trivial control command and once with the stronger direct `UuidCreateSequential` plus `NtAllocateUuids` burst. Both runs reached `probe-stage = exception`, produced result text, and then failed with `Procmon SaveAs timed out after 60 second(s).`, which narrows the remaining exact-read gap to a Procmon export limitation rather than trigger identity.

records.name: Threaded DPCs
records.summary: Officially documented threaded-DPC control. Microsoft documents ThreadDpcEnable under HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\SessionManager\Kernel, states that threaded DPCs are enabled by default, and says setting the value to 0 disables them. The app writes 1 on the documented path as an explicit enabled-state reset, and a bounded Win25H2Clean VM suite exercised the `0` state through real reboot, CPU and memory workloads, and restore back to the missing baseline.

decision.why: Microsoft documents the exact path, says threaded DPCs are enabled by default, and states that setting the value to 0 disables them. The app writes 1 on that same path as an explicit enabled-state reset, and the bounded Win25H2Clean VM suite exercised the disable state and restored the missing baseline cleanly. That is enough to treat the app's explicit enabled-state reset as app-ready while still keeping it out of general-user presets.

app_current_implementation.notes: The current app research-surface manifest defaults this card to ThreadDpcEnable = 1, preserving the documented threaded-DPC-enabled state while keeping the record_id bound to the surfaced card.

records.name: Disable Exception Chain Validation
records.summary: Validated cross-layer record for DisableExceptionChainValidation under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel. The broad 96-key phase-0 batch confirmed the baseline path and value absence, repo system notes already tracked the value by name, broad current-build static triage found an exact ntoskrnl.exe hit, and the tools-hardened Session Manager Kernel lightweight ETW batch wrote the candidate, rebooted once, and captured exact RegQueryValue hits for DisableExceptionChainValidation while the other 20 sibling kernel candidates stayed at zero exact-target hits. A later source-enrichment follow-up on public `systeminformer/phnt` headers then added a small but useful corroboration by surfacing the `DisableExceptionChainValidation` execution-option bit in `ntpsapi.h`. That is enough for Class A in this project even though the value remains research-only and not app-mapped.

decision.why: DisableExceptionChainValidation now has converged project evidence on the tools-hardened baseline: broad phase-0 existence, repo system notes, a current-build ntoskrnl static hit, and an exact early-boot runtime read from the single-reboot Session Manager Kernel ETW batch. The value remains research-only and not app-mapped, but that no longer blocks Class A.

Decompiled OsEventsTimestampInterval still explains the companion TimeStampInterval cadence, the 24-hour cap, and the current-version fallback path, while the 25H2 Procmon and Ghidra follow-up keeps the current-build DiagTrack lead and adjacent Reliability\PBR runtime read in repo evidence.

records.name: Classic Context Menu on Windows 11
records.summary: The current app still matches the original Microsoft Q&A HKCU workaround for the Windows 11 classic context menu by creating HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\{86ca1aa0-34aa-4e8b-a509-50c905bae2a2}\InprocServer32 with an empty default value. That same Q&A thread is now internally contradictory on newer builds: some later replies say the workaround is deprecated in 24H2, while other later replies still report success when the command is run elevated and Explorer is restarted. Comment-level HKLM ownership/edit advice also appears in the thread, but this review keeps RegProbe on the lower-risk HKCU workaround and does not adopt the HKLM ownership path as canonical research.

decision.why: The app still matches the HKCU add/delete workaround shown in the current Microsoft Q&A article body, and the repo documents the restore story. The same official thread is now internally contradictory on newer 24H2-era behavior, and comment-level HKLM ownership/edit advice conflicts with the app's current low-risk HKCU mapping. This therefore remains workaround evidence rather than a stable Microsoft policy contract.
